title: Lester's taste in saxophonists: Trumbauer over Bud Freeman
summary: Phillips says no one was playing what Lester wanted to hear on saxophone; he disliked Bud Freeman and Trumbauer was his main man.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You mentioned already the Red Nichols records, "Dinah" and "The Five Pennies." But any other particular records that were especially important to Lester, that he was particularly
fond of? You on another occasion told me about 'Singing The Blues.' Any other records that you can remember...?

There wasn't nobody playing nothin' in them days. Not on no saxophone. And playing nothin' that he wanted to hear. But he sounded better... Most people was moaning on saxophone then. A tenor player didn't never... Only cats that played solos on sax then was alto. Tenor didn't play nothin'. He said, 'MMMM...' -- moan, you know what I mean? He didn't play nothin' (?). Well, Bud Freeman, he was playing like that, but...
Did Lester ever listen to him back then?
No. He didn't care nothin' about Bud.
He didn't go for Bud Freeman.

He didn't like Bud. But he's still out there, too, Bud is. But he didn't like that kind of playing. He didn't like Bud. He liked Frankie Trumbauer. I'd sure like to have seen him stay... He quit playing. I mean, he retired from music. He got an airplane. I think he got killed in the airplane or something.
Yeah, in '56. So he was under Frankie Trumbauer, you're saying.
Yeah. Well, see, everything you'd hear then was Frankie Trumbauer, saxophone...
In other words, there wasn't much else.
No, there wasn't much else. If you had...
